title: Stock Market Today, Nov. 2: CoreWeave Slides on Debt Concerns After CrowdStrike Partnership Expands
detail:
Stock Market Today, Nov. 2: CoreWeave Slides on Debt Concerns After CrowdStrike Partnership Expands
Will Healy, The Motley Fool
Mon, November 2, 2026 at 4:00 PM MST 3 min read
CRWV
CRWD
^GSPC
^IXIC
ORCL
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

CoreWeave (NASDAQ:CRWV), a specialized cloud computing provider for generative AI workloads, closed at $50.15, down 8.60%. Premarket partnership news with CrowdStrike faded as leverage concerns weighed on the market, and investors are watching Nov. 10 earnings.

Trading volume reached 47.1M shares, coming in nearly 21% above its three-month average of 38.9M shares. CoreWeave IPO'd in 2025 and has grown 25% since going public.

How the markets moved today

The S&P 500 (SNPINDEX: ^GSPC) dropped 0.50% to 7,542, and the Nasdaq Composite (NASDAQINDEX: ^IXIC) fell 1.07% to 25,164. Among peers in AI cloud infrastructure and specialized data center services, Oracle closed at $119.10, down 8.85%, and Nebius Group closed at $141.39, down 8.27%, underscoring weakness across chip-adjacent infrastructure names.

What this means for investors

The latest price action in CoreWeave shows continued shareholder discomfort with the cloud stock's reliance on debt.

Although the expanded partnership with CrowdStrike is objectively good news for the company, the excitement over that deal was short-lived as the stock's downtrend continued.

Customer interest is not the issue. Demand for neocloud infrastructure is insatiable, as CoreWeave's backlog totaled $104 billion, not including Q3 customer commitments.

Still, that demand does the company little good if its ability to finance infrastructure builds remains in question. Considering that industry insiders like Elon Musk think many neoclouds will fail, CoreWeave is likely to remain under the gun for the foreseeable future.

In fairness, CoreWeave is not the only neocloud stock struggling, as both Nebius and Oracle also plunged. However, Oracle still has other legacy businesses, and Nebius is a profitable company with a debt level that's a fraction of CoreWeave's approximate $35 billion in obligations.

The real test for CoreWeave stock may come when it announces its earnings for the third quarter of 2026 on Nov. 10. Factors such as growth, capital expenditures, and debt levels will be where investors will probably focus.

If CoreWeave can continue building infrastructure, address its backlog, and service its debt, it may eventually win back investors' confidence. Nonetheless, any interruptions to this growth could be costly for CoreWeave, making investing in the stock a risky proposition at this time.

title: 63% Upside for Oracle? Stephens Thinks So, and Here’s How
detail:
63% Upside for Oracle? Stephens Thinks So, and Here’s How
Roxanna Maglangit

ORCL
OPAI.PVT
Trade Oracle on Coinbase
Trading disclosure
63% Upside for Oracle? Stephens Thinks So, and Here's How ©@yhelfman via Canva, @Yurich84 from Getty Images via Canva
Key Takeaways

Stephens upgraded Oracle to Overweight on Monday and raised its price target to $213, 63% above Friday's close.

Stephens' case rests on Oracle's Investor Day, where the company put a date on positive free cash flow and capped new fundraising at $20 billion through fiscal 2030.

To reach the target, investors would have to pay 25x Oracle's expected earnings over the next twelve months, above its 21x five-year average, though analysts expect earnings to jump in fiscal 2028.

Stephens' target looks about right if fiscal 2028's earnings arrive, but OpenAI's share of Oracle's backlog is the risk the funding plan leaves open.

Oracle (ORCL:NYSE) closed Friday at $130.68, 50% below its high of a year ago. On Monday, Stephens upgraded it to Overweight from Equal Weight and raised its price target to $213 from $185, 63% above Friday's close.

The build ate the cash

In fiscal 2026, the year to May 31, Oracle spent $55.7 billion on capex for its AI build, and free cash flow was negative $23.7 billion.

Its Sept. 10 release showed negative free cash flow of $5 billion on $28.5 billion of first-quarter capex. Asked on the call when free cash flow would turn positive, CFO Hilary Maxson said: "We haven't given a particular time frame on that yet, and we don't expect to give that today."

Stephens says the money is lined up

Oracle gave a time frame at its Oct. 28 Investor Day: positive free cash flow in the second half of fiscal 2028. It also capped new fundraising at $20 billion through fiscal 2030, split evenly between stock and debt.

Stephens says vendor financing, customers' own hardware and prepayments now cover more of the build, so Oracle needs about $20 billion of new funding, about half of what was expected before.

Does $213 hold up?

The average target of the 43 analysts covering Oracle fell from $348 on Nov. 4, 2025, to $236 on Oct. 30, with individual targets ranging from $110 to $400. Stephens' $213 sits 10% below that average:

Oracle (ORCL): analysts' consensus (mean) price target, $ per share, last year (TIKR)

Analysts expect normalized EPS of $8.14 in fiscal 2027 and $11.04 in fiscal 2028, up from $8.05 and $10.89 three months ago:

Oracle (ORCL): normalized EPS, actual and consensus estimates, $ per share, fiscal 2024-2028 (years to May) (TIKR)

Yet the stock trades at 15x forward earnings, well below its five-year average of 21x:

Oracle (ORCL): forward (NTM) P/E, last 5 years (TIKR)

Investors paid about that much from 2014 to 2021, when Oracle's revenue grew about 1% a year. Oracle now guides to at least 34% revenue growth in fiscal 2027.

title: Oracle Sinks 7% on $20 Billion Stock and Bond Sale to Fund AI Buildout

Oracle Sinks 7% on $20 Billion Stock and Bond Sale to Fund AI Buildout
David Hanson

ORCL
Trade Oracle on Coinbase

Oracle Sinks 7% on $20 Billion Stock and Bond Sale to Fund AI Buildout ©v2killer7603 from pixabay and spxChrome from Getty Images Signature DanielPrudek from Getty Images and Burak The Weekender from Pexels Bianca Constantinescu's Images and Madalina Vasilica's Imags from Canva
Key Takeaways

Oracle shares fell 7% today after it filed to sell $10 billion of common stock and $10 billion of senior notes.

The sale uses up the $20 billion cap on new raises through fiscal 2030, the cap that sent the stock up 12% last week.

Half of it is new stock, on top of the $19.9 billion of shares Oracle sold from February to August.

The dilution is small. What matters now is whether Oracle turns free cash flow positive in the second half of fiscal 2028 without raising again.

Oracle (ORCL:NYSE) is down 7% today. Before the open, it filed to sell $10 billion of common stock and $10 billion of senior notes.

Nobody should be surprised by the raise. At last Wednesday's Investor Day, Oracle capped new capital raises at $20 billion through fiscal 2030, split evenly between stock and debt, and the stock jumped 12% the next day.

Stephens even upgraded Oracle to Overweight this morning. It raised its target to $213 from $185, arguing that Investor Day had answered the funding questions. Oracle's shelf filing came 23 minutes later.

Talk about timing.

TIKR tracks 43 analysts on Oracle. How many say "Buy"?

See the full breakdown of Buy, Hold, and Sell ratings on Oracle, along with Wall Street's revenue and earnings estimates, all in one place. More than 500,000 investors use TIKR to research stocks like this one. See Oracle's Analyst Ratings

Long way to go

That $20 billion is supposed to carry Oracle through the peak of its spending. Management forecast positive free cash flow in the second half of fiscal 2028 and more than $30 billion of it in fiscal 2029, once capex peaks in fiscal 2027 and 2028.

That's a long climb from negative $23.7 billion of free cash flow in fiscal 2026. Analysts' estimates show how far Oracle still has to go:

Oracle (ORCL): free cash flow, actual and consensus estimates, $ billions, fiscal 2024-2029 (years to May) (TIKR)
Selling stock at a discount

The new stock is worth less than 3% of Oracle's market value, and I'd take that over $20 billion more of bonds. Oracle's total debt, leases included, was $169.1 billion at Aug. 31, more than double the $75.9 billion it had in fiscal 2022.

S&P cut Oracle to BBB- in July, one step above junk. Its credit default swaps now trade more like a high-end junk rating, according to S&P Global Market Intelligence's Gavan Nolan. Keeping the investment-grade rating is worth a little dilution.

The catch is the price. Oracle traded at 15x forward earnings at Friday's close, against a five-year average of 21x:

Oracle (ORCL): forward (NTM) P/E, last 5 years (TIKR)

At this morning's price, it's about 14x.

Oracle has no room left to miss

I suspect the real worry for investors is that Oracle has nothing left under its own cap. Still, if the free cash flow plan holds, a stock at about 14x forward earnings looks cheap to me.

How Oracle's $20 billion stock and debt raise breaks down

Oracle will split the raise in two: $10 billion of new common stock and $10 billion of senior notes. Oracle says the cash is meant for capital spending as well as paying down other debts and "future investments or acquisitions."

While the stock is getting hit today, this isn't a shock. Just last week, Oracle said it would raise additional funding for its AI build-out -- no more than $20 billion through fiscal 2030. Still, it seems investors are still unsure about the additional raise.

Image source: Getty Images.

Why I'm not sold on Oracle's AI spending limit

If Oracle can limit itself to this raise for the next few years, it would help calm fears over the sustainability of its substantial AI bets. I'm not entirely convinced it will, and I fear capital spending could expand while, at the same time, revenues are delayed as data center projects hit snags in construction and political opposition.

title: Can Workday Stock Get Back To Where It Was?
detail:
Can Workday Stock Get Back To Where It Was?
Trefis Team

Workday (WDAY) shares peaked in February 2024, and the close on October 30, 2026 left the stock more than a third below that level. It is natural to keep measuring the shares against that old price, treating the peak as where Workday belongs and today's price as the exception. How big a climb would it take to get back there?

Workday Stock Needs A 55% Gain To Get Back

Workday stock currently trades 35.6% below its February 2024 high, meaning the shares need a 55.3% gain from today's price to reclaim that level. Even if the climb took three years, it would require an annual return of 15.8%. That is the bar you set for the stock when you wait for the old high.

Has Workday Stock Ever Gained 55% In Three Years?

Yes. Over the last ten years, the stock gained 55.3% or more in 34.6% of all rolling three-year periods measured from every single trading day. That climb fits within Workday's own record, but the shares fell short of it in most of those stretches.

What Has Waiting Cost Workday Holders?

The wait has already lasted 2.7 years. During that span, Workday stock is down 35.6% before dividends, while the S&P 500 is up 49.5%, also before dividends. A holder waiting out the decline has absorbed the drop in Workday's price and missed the market's gain over the same years.

Is Workday The Same Business It Was Then?

Workday operates as a larger business today than it did at its high in February 2024.

Workday runs a platform for HR, finance, and IT, with subscription services bringing in 92.5% of its revenue in fiscal 2026. Revenue over the twelve months to July 2026 is up 39.9% from the twelve months to January 2024.

Profit from running the business grew faster than sales, and the operating margin climbed from 2.5% to 12.0% over the same span. Net income is a little lower than it was then. Both totals include tax benefits, about $1.05 billion in the quarter to January 2024 and $305 million in the quarter to July 2026.

Workday is a bigger company today and maintains a wider operating margin, yet its stock is lower. The question worth asking about Workday is not when its stock gets back to that price, but whether 4.8 times its sales over the past twelve months, against 3.2 for the S&P 500, is a fair price for the business it is today. That price follows an August 13, 2026 Reuters report that Silver Lake was in talks to buy Workday, which lifted the shares 17.8% that day.
